authority: Esso Australia Resources Ltd v Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1999) 201 CLR 49

edge_tested: purpose_test_historical (sole→dominant; do NOT label outcome under sole-purpose)
document: Internal reports prepared by hospital staff following the death of a patient, produced pursuant to the hospital authority's standing practice of reporting such incidents
parties_roles: Plaintiff (administratrix / widow of the deceased patient) suing the State of New South Wales in negligence; the State, as operator of the psychiatric hospital, claimed privilege over its employees' reports, which were routed in part to its legal advisers
purpose: The reports served several concurrent purposes — internal hospital administration and review of the incident as well as possible use by the authority's legal advisers in anticipated litigation. No one purpose predominated; they would have been brought into existence regardless of any prospect of litigation
basis: Routine multi-purpose internal corporate reports are not privileged: a document created to serve two or more purposes of comparable weight is not brought into existence for the requisite privileged purpose. The majority expressed this as a sole purpose test; that test was later displaced by the dominant purpose test in Esso, which declined to follow Grant v Downs on the sole-versus-dominant point (the point was never argued in Grant). The document result stands under either test — reports of this kind fail the dominant purpose test as well
notes: Determination is the document outcome, not an endorsement of the sole-purpose test — per reconstruction note item 2, the test is discarded and the result kept (multi-purpose internal reports fail dominant purpose too, Esso [38], [60]). Esso pinpoints are from the worked Esso record's session, not verified here. Do not describe Grant as "overruled"

document: Documents concerning a client's affairs held by the client's solicitors, accepted to be the subject of legal advice privilege, which police sought to seize under a search warrant issued under s 10 of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth)
parties_roles: Client and the solicitors holding the client's documents, resisting execution of the warrant; Commonwealth police officer as the party who obtained the warrant in aid of a criminal investigation
purpose: The documents were confidential communications between client and solicitor for the purpose of giving or obtaining legal advice; the privileged character of the communications themselves was not the contested question — the fight was over whether privilege operated outside court proceedings
basis: Legal professional privilege is not a mere rule of evidence confined to judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings; it is a doctrine of substance that can be asserted against the exercise of coercive statutory powers, including search warrants. A statute displaces it only by express words or necessary implication, and the general words of s 10 did not do so — so documents subject to the privilege could not lawfully be seized under the warrant. The Court (by majority, 4:3) departed from the narrower view that privilege operated only in curial contexts
notes: Edge is the extension of privilege beyond the courtroom as a substantive right, not the purpose test. Confident of the holding, the s 10 Crimes Act warrant context, the 4:3 division, and the departure from the earlier curial-only view (O'Reilly); the precise underlying investigation and the composition of the majority are deliberately not asserted — not certain enough of those details

document: Copies of pre-existing original documents, where the originals were not themselves privileged, but the copies were brought into existence for the purpose of obtaining legal advice or for use in litigation; the copies were held at solicitors' premises and were sought under search warrants
parties_roles: Australian Federal Police executing search warrants in aid of an investigation; the companies under investigation and their solicitors claiming privilege over the copy documents in the solicitors' possession
purpose: The copies were made for the privileged purpose — communication with legal advisers for advice or for use in litigation — while the originals had been created for other, non-privileged business purposes
basis: Privilege protects communications rather than pieces of paper as such, so the question is asked of each document separately: a copy made for the requisite privileged purpose can itself be privileged even though the original is not, because the act of copying and assembling documents for submission to a lawyer is part of the privileged communication. The unprivileged character of the original is not inherited by the copy; what matters is the purpose for which the copy was brought into existence
authority: Commissioner of Australian Federal Police v Propend Finance Pty Ltd (1997) 188 CLR 501
notes: Decided under the sole purpose test then in force (pre-Esso); the copy-document principle now operates with dominant purpose as the threshold. The Court divided and the individual judgments differ in reasoning — confident of the majority outcome and the principle as stated, but the composition of the majority and the precise formulation in any single judgment are not asserted. AFP warrant / investigation context asserted at a general level only

determination: privileged (in principle — third-party authorship no bar; see notes)
document: A valuation/financial analysis prepared by the client's accountants at the client's request, provided to the client for the purpose of being passed to the client's lawyers as the basis for obtaining legal advice on a taxation matter
parties_roles: Taxpayer companies claiming privilege; the Commissioner of Taxation seeking access to documents under statutory information-gathering powers; the accounting firm as third-party author, not itself the client's lawyer and not retained by the lawyers
purpose: The client commissioned the third-party document in order to communicate its substance to its legal advisers to obtain legal advice; the accountants' role was to equip the client to make that privileged communication
basis: Legal advice privilege can attach to a document prepared by a third party who is not the client's agent for the purpose of communicating with the lawyer. The older view that a third party's document is protected only if the third party acted as a mere conduit or communication agent was rejected: what matters is the client's purpose in procuring the document — if the dominant purpose for its creation was its use in a communication to the lawyer to obtain advice, privilege can attach even though its author stood outside the lawyer–client relationship
authority: Pratt Holdings Pty Ltd v Commissioner of Taxation (2004) 136 FCR 357
notes: Confident of the principle and that the Full Court rejected the "agent for communication" requirement, reversing the narrower approach taken below; this is the proposition the case is cited for. Less certain of the precise disposition of the specific documents (whether the Full Court finally ruled them privileged or remitted the purpose question for determination) — left unasserted, check on primary-source review. Accountant identified generically, not by firm name

determination: UNCERTAIN — cited for its enumeration of protected categories; document-level outcomes not reliably recalled (see notes)
document: Not a single document: the judgment addresses classes of communications. The privilege claims arose over documents sought in proceedings brought by the Trade Practices Commission
parties_roles: Trade Practices Commission as the party seeking production; the respondent parties claiming legal professional privilege over documents held by them or their solicitors
purpose: Various by category — the judgment's significance is its catalogue of the kinds of communications that attract privilege under both limbs, rather than a single purpose finding
basis: The judgment (Lockhart J) sets out a non-exhaustive enumeration of the classes of communications protected: communications between client and lawyer made for the purpose of obtaining or giving legal advice; the lawyer's advice to the client; communications between the client's lawyer and third parties made for the purpose of existing or reasonably anticipated litigation; communications between the client and third parties made for the purpose of being laid before the lawyer for advice or for use in litigation; the lawyer's own notes, memoranda and working papers brought into existence for advice or litigation purposes; and briefs and instructions to counsel. Each category remains subject to the confidentiality and purpose requirements
authority: Trade Practices Commission v Sterling (1979) 36 FLR 244
notes: Determination marked UNCERTAIN deliberately: the taxonomy is what this row tests and it is the case's standing contribution, but the ruling on each contested document is not recalled from memory, and a fluent guess would violate the drafting rules. Decided under the sole purpose regime (post-Grant, pre-Esso), so the purpose threshold attached to the categories has since changed to dominant purpose. The category list is a from-memory paraphrase — the exact number and wording of Lockhart J's categories must come from the judgment on primary-source review

determination: privileged — privilege over the underlying source materials not waived
document: Source documents and working papers assembled by the claimants' legal advisers in preparing a "claim book" for an Aboriginal land claim, where the claim book itself had been lodged and made available in the proceeding and the underlying materials were then sought
parties_roles: Aboriginal land claimants as privilege holders, their legal advisers having compiled the claim book; the Attorney-General for the Northern Territory as opposing party seeking the underlying documents in proceedings before the Aboriginal Land Commissioner
purpose: The materials were brought together and worked up by the claimants' lawyers to prepare and advance the claimants' case in the land claim — a use squarely within the privilege
basis: Two propositions. First, legal professional privilege is a substantive protection of the client, not a mere rule of evidence confined to courtrooms, so it could be invoked in the statutory inquiry before the Land Commissioner. Second, deploying the claim book did not impliedly waive privilege in the source materials: implied waiver turns on whether the privilege holder's conduct is inconsistent with maintaining the confidentiality of the underlying communications, judged by considerations of fairness, and lodging the claim book did not make it unfair for the claimants to withhold the materials from which it was compiled
notes: Confident of the no-waiver outcome, the fairness-based approach to implied waiver (later refined in Mann v Carnell), and the substantive-right characterisation this row's edge tests. Less certain of procedural specifics — which land claim and the exact posture in which the question reached the High Court — so those are stated generically. The case does double duty as a waiver authority; the golden-set edge here is the substantive-right point, so basis leads with it

determination: privileged — no exception even for an accused seeking material for the defence of criminal charges
document: Documents held by a firm of solicitors recording or evidencing communications with a client of the firm, sought by subpoena by an accused person in criminal proceedings who contended the documents would assist his defence
parties_roles: The accused as the party seeking production; the solicitors' firm resisting production of its client's communications, the privilege belonging to the client rather than to either the firm or the accused
purpose: The communications arose in the ordinary course of a lawyer–client relationship for the purpose of giving or obtaining legal advice; their privileged character was not the real contest — the question was whether the privilege must yield to a competing interest
basis: Legal professional privilege, once it attaches, is not subject to case-by-case balancing against other interests, even an interest as weighty as an accused's ability to defend criminal charges. The privilege rests on the client's freedom to make full and frank disclosure to their lawyer, which serves the administration of justice as a whole; that rationale requires a rule certain in operation, and an exception allowing privileged material to be reached whenever it might assist an accused would leave clients unable to rely on the protection when communicating. The majority therefore declined to recognise an "innocence" or defence exception
authority: Carter v Northmore Hale Davy & Leake (1995) 183 CLR 121
notes: Confident of the outcome and the no-balancing/absoluteness proposition, which is the scope point this row's edge tests. The Court divided and there were substantial dissents favouring some exception for an accused — which Justices fell on which side is not asserted. The underlying facts (nature of the charges, the client whose privilege it was) are stated generically; sharpen from the judgment on primary-source review

determination: n/a — not a privilege determination; rule-statement authority for the meaning of "dominant purpose"
document: None in privilege terms. The case is a Part IVA Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 tax avoidance matter concerning an offshore short-term investment arrangement; no privilege claim was in issue
parties_roles: Commissioner of Taxation against taxpayer companies; no lawyer–client communication was the subject of the dispute
purpose: n/a as a document-purpose finding. The case's contribution is definitional: what "dominant" means when a test turns on a dominant purpose held among several coexisting purposes
basis: In construing the statutory phrase "dominant purpose", the High Court treated "dominant" as meaning the ruling, prevailing or most influential purpose — a purpose can be dominant without being the sole purpose, and the presence of other purposes (there, a commercial profit-making purpose alongside the tax purpose) does not prevent one purpose from predominating. Esso later adopted this meaning of "dominant" for the legal professional privilege dominant purpose test, which is why a non-privilege case sits in this set

notes: record_type=rule — scores as rule-statement, not determination; harness must exclude from Gate 1 scoring. Confident that Spotless is the source Esso drew on for the meaning of "dominant" and that the taxpayers lost on the Part IVA question (dominant purpose of obtaining a tax benefit found). determination: UNCERTAIN as to the disposition of the specific documents — confident of the principle (privilege can attach to advice from a foreign lawyer, with independence not a free-standing additional requirement) but not of how the appeal was finally resolved on the facts (see notes)
document: Notes and records of a meeting between an Australian client and a Swiss lawyer consulted in Switzerland, over which privilege was claimed in Australian proceedings
parties_roles: The client who consulted the Swiss lawyer as privilege claimant; the opposing party in Australian litigation challenging the claim on the ground, among others, that the adviser was not an Australian-admitted lawyer and that independent legal advice was not shown
purpose: Contested — the challenge put in issue whether the consultation was for the dominant purpose of obtaining legal advice as opposed to business purposes, and the purpose finding was central to the outcome at first instance
basis: Australian common law privilege is not confined to communications with lawyers admitted in Australia: communications with a foreign lawyer acting in the capacity of an independent professional legal adviser are capable of attracting privilege. The Full Federal Court treated the lawyer's independence and professional character not as an extra element the claimant must separately prove in every case, but as an aspect of the ordinary question whether the communication was a confidential communication with a legal adviser acting in that capacity, for the requisite dominant purpose
notes: Determination marked UNCERTAIN under rule 4: the trial judge refused the privilege claim over the meeting notes, and the Full Court corrected aspects of the reasoning on foreign lawyers and independence, but whether the appeal ultimately succeeded or the refusal stood on the dominant purpose facts is not recalled with confidence — resolve on primary-source review. The principle stated in basis is what the case is cited for and what this row's edge tests

determination: privileged — legal advice given by salaried government lawyers is capable of attracting privilege, and the claim was upheld in principle for the advice documents in issue
document: Documents recording legal advice given within the Commonwealth government by lawyers employed in its legal service, access to which was sought under the Freedom of Information Act 1982 (Cth), with the government relying on the exemption for documents subject to legal professional privilege
parties_roles: An FOI applicant seeking access to government documents; the Commonwealth as privilege holder; the advisers were salaried government-employed lawyers rather than external counsel or private solicitors
purpose: The communications were made for the purpose of giving or obtaining legal advice within government — advice sought by the client agency from its legal advisers in their professional capacity
basis: A salaried employment relationship does not of itself exclude legal professional privilege. Advice given by government lawyers attracts privilege where the adviser acts in a professional capacity as a lawyer, with the independence and professional obligations that characterise the lawyer–client relationship, notwithstanding that the "client" is the employer. The lawyer–client relationship can exist between a government agency and its own legal service, and privilege then operates in the FOI context through the exemption for privileged documents
notes: Confident of the core capacity holding — this is the authority the engine's capacity rule rests on, and the salaried-lawyer point is what the edge tests. The judgments diverge on the precise qualification required of the adviser (admission, practising certificate, or competence-and-independence formulations differ between Justices) — that spread is real and matters for the rule layer, so pin the formulations to specific judgments on primary-source review rather than trusting any single phrasing here. Whether every individual document in the FOI request was ultimately held exempt is not asserted

determination: UNCERTAIN as to the outcome for the specific report — recollection leans to the privilege claim failing, but not firmly enough to assert; the anticipation-of-litigation test the case states is the confident part (see notes)
document: An investigation report prepared on behalf of the employer following a workplace accident, over which litigation privilege was claimed on the basis that litigation arising from the accident was anticipated when the report was commissioned
parties_roles: Mitsubishi Electric Australia as the employer/privilege claimant; the Victorian WorkCover Authority as the party seeking the report in connection with proceedings arising from the workplace injury
purpose: Contested on both elements of the litigation limb: whether, at the time the report was brought into existence, litigation was reasonably anticipated, and whether use in that litigation was the dominant purpose as against concurrent purposes such as investigating the cause of the accident and preventing recurrence
basis: The Court of Appeal's contribution is the standard for anticipated litigation: litigation is "anticipated" for privilege purposes when there is a real prospect of litigation, as distinct from a mere possibility — but it does not need to be more likely than not. That threshold then combines with the Esso dominant purpose test: the claimant must show both the real prospect at the time of creation and that use in the apprehended litigation was the dominant purpose of bringing the document into existence
authority: Mitsubishi Electric Australia Pty Ltd v Victorian WorkCover Authority (2002) 4 VR 332
notes: Determination marked UNCERTAIN under rule 4. Confident of the "real prospect, not mere possibility, need not be more likely than not" formulation (Batt JA) and that the case applies Esso dominant purpose to an anticipated-litigation claim — that is the edge this row tests. Not confident of the disposition: recollection leans to the report failing (mixed investigative purposes), but the procedural posture and the party relationships (insurer/VWA role, which proceeding the report was sought in) are not reliably recalled and are stated generically. determination: Mixed, category-dependent — the ruling sorts expert-related documents into privileged and unprivileged classes rather than giving a single up-or-down holding (see basis; specific document outcomes not asserted)
document: Documents connected with expert witnesses in civil proceedings brought by ASIC: briefs and instructions provided to experts, material supplied to them, and the experts' own working papers and draft reports
parties_roles: ASIC as regulator prosecuting civil proceedings against Southcorp; Southcorp asserting privilege over expert-related documents; the experts as third parties retained for the litigation
purpose: The expert communications and materials were brought into existence for the dominant purpose of use in the conduct of the litigation — the litigation limb was engaged; the dispute was over which categories of expert material the privilege actually covers and what is lost by deploying a report
basis: The judgment (Lindgren J) states the propositions since applied as the standard framework: confidential communications between a party or its lawyers and an expert retained for litigation — briefs, instructions, documents provided to the expert — attract litigation privilege as communications made for the dominant purpose of the litigation. But the expert's own working documents, notes and drafts are ordinarily not privileged, because privilege protects communications, not the expert's independent work product. And where an expert's report is served or deployed, privilege in the instructions and material on which the report is based will ordinarily be waived, since fairness prevents a party relying on the opinion while withholding what shaped it
authority: Australian Securities & Investments Commission v Southcorp Ltd (2003) 130 FCR 406
notes: Confident of the three-part framework — it is what the case is universally cited for and what the edge tests. The framework is a from-memory paraphrase of Lindgren J's numbered propositions; verify the exact enumeration and paragraph pinpoint on primary-source review. How each specific contested document fell out in the ruling, and the precise subject matter of the underlying ASIC proceedings, are not asserted
